segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: I’ve still got loads to do for our report on nutritional food labels.

segments.speaker: ALICE
segments.en: Me too. What did you learn from doing the project about your own shopping habits?

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: Well, I’ve always had to check labels for traces of peanuts in everything I eat because of my allergy. But beyond that I’ve never really been concerned enough to check how healthy a product is.

segments.speaker: ALICE
segments.en: This project has actually taught me to read the labels much more carefully. I tended to believe claims on packaging like ‘low in fat’. But I now realise that the ‘healthy’ yoghurt I’ve bought for years is full of sugar and that it’s actually quite high in calories.

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: Ready meals are the worst ... comparing the labels on supermarket pizzas was a real eye-opener. Did you have any idea how many calories they contain? I was amazed.

segments.speaker: ALICE
segments.en: Yes, because unless you read the label really carefully, you wouldn’t know that the nutritional values given are for half a pizza.

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: When most people eat the whole pizza. Not exactly transparent is it?

segments.speaker: ALICE
segments.en: Not at all. But I expect it won’t stop you from buying pizza?

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: Probably not, no! I thought comparing the different labelling systems used by food manufactures was interesting. I think the kind of labelling system used makes a big difference.

segments.speaker: ALICE
segments.en: Which one did you prefer?

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: I liked the traditional daily value system best – the one which tells you what proportion of your required daily intake of each ingredient the product contains. I’m not sure it’s the easiest for people to use but at least you get the full story. I like to know all the ingredients in a product – not just how much fat, salt and sugar they contain.

segments.speaker: ALICE
segments.en: But it’s good supermarkets have been making an effort to provide reliable information for customers.

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: Yes. There just needs to be more consistency between labelling systems used by different supermarkets, in terms of portion sizes, etc.

segments.speaker: ALICE
segments.en: Mmm. The labels on the different brands of chicken flavour crisps were quite revealing too, weren’t they?

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: Yeah. I don’t understand how they can get away with calling them chicken flavour when they only contain artificial additives.

segments.speaker: ALICE
segments.en: I know. I’d at least have expected them to contain a small percentage of real chicken.

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: Absolutely.

segments.speaker: ALICE
segments.en: I think having nutritional food labeling has been a good idea, don’t you? I think it will change people’s behaviour and stop mothers, in particular, buying the wrong things.

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: But didn’t that study kind of prove the opposite? People didn’t necessarily stop buying unhealthy products.

segments.speaker: ALICE
segments.en: They only said that might be the case. Those findings weren’t that conclusive and it was quite a small-scale study. I think more research has to be done.

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: Yes, I think you’re probably right. ——————–

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: What do you think of the traffic-light system?

segments.speaker: ALICE
segments.en: I think supermarkets like the idea of having a colour-coded system – red, orange or green – for levels of fat, sugar and salt in a product.

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: But it’s not been adopted universally ( &28). And not on all products. Why do you suppose that is?

segments.speaker: ALICE
segments.en: Pressure from the food manufacturers. Hardly surprising that some of them are opposed to flagging up how unhealthy their products are.

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: I’d have thought it would have been compulsory. It seems ridiculous it isn’t.

segments.speaker: ALICE
segments.en: I know. And what I couldn’t get over is the fact that it was brought in without enough consultation – a lot of experts had deep reservations about it.

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: That is a bit weird. I suppose there’s an argument for doing the research now when consumers are familiar with this system.

segments.speaker: ALICE
segments.en: Yeah, maybe.

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: The participants in the survey were quite positive about the traffic-light system.

segments.speaker: ALICE
segments.en: Mmm. But I don’t think they targeted the right people. They should have focused on people with low literacy levels because these labels are designed to be accessible to them.

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: Yeah. But it’s good to get feedback from all socio-economic groups ( &30). And there wasn’t much variation in their responses.

segments.speaker: ALICE
segments.en: No. But if they hadn’t interviewed participants face-to-face, they could have used a much bigger sample size. I wonder why they chose that method?

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: Dunno. How were they selected? Did they volunteer or were they approached?

segments.speaker: ALICE
segments.en: I think they volunteered. The thing that wasn’t stated was how often they bought packaged food – all we know is how frequently they used the supermarket.

instructions: Complete the original Cambridge IELTS listening questions below.
questions.source_text:
SECTION 3
Questions 21-30
LABELS GIVING NUTRITIONAL INFORMATION ON FOOD PACKAGING
Choose the correct letter A, B or C.
Questions:
    Q Num: 21
    Text: What was Jack's attitude to nutritional food labels before this project?
    Options:
        He didn't read everything on them.
        He didn't think they were important.
        He thought they were too complicated.
    Q Num: 22
    Text: Alice says that before doing this project,
    Options:
        she was unaware of what certain foods contained.
        she was too lazy to read food labels.
        she was only interested in the number of calories.
    Q Num: 23
    Text: When discussing supermarket brands of pizza, Jack agrees with Alice that
    Options:
        the list of ingredients is shocking.
        he will hesitate before buying pizza again.
        the nutritional label is misleading.
    Q Num: 24
    Text: Jack prefers the daily value system to other labelling systems because it is
    Options:
        more accessible.
        more logical.
        more comprehensive.
    Q Num: 25
    Text: What surprised both students about one flavour of crisps?
    Options:
        The percentage of artificial additives given was incorrect.
        The products did not contain any meat.
        The labels did not list all the ingredients.
    Q Num: 26
    Text: What do the students think about research into the impact of nutritional food labelling?
    Options:
        It did not produce clear results.
        It focused on the wrong people.
        It made unrealistic recommendations.
Choose TWO letters A–E.
Q Num: 27
Text: Which TWO things surprised the students about the traffic-light system for nutritional labels?
Count: 2
Options:
    Id: A
    Text: its widespread use
    Id: B
    Text: the fact that it is voluntary for supermarkets
    Id: C
    Text: how little research was done before its introduction
    Id: D
    Text: its unpopularity with food manufacturers
    Id: E
    Text: the way that certain colours are used
Choose TWO letters A–E.
Q Num: 29
Text: Which TWO things are true about the participants in the study on the traffic-light system?
Count: 2
Options:
    Id: A
    Text: They had low literacy levels.
    Id: B
    Text: They were regular consumers of packaged food.
    Id: C
    Text: They were selected randomly.
    Id: D
    Text: They were from all socio-economic groups.
    Id: E
    Text: They were interviewed face-to-face.
